title: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It can be shown, at least as a very common rule, that those eggs which are most unsymmetrical, or most tapered off posteriorly, are also eggs of a large size relatively to the parent bird.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XV, “On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures”; topic “Egg size and asymmetry”. Scope: birds' eggs across species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch15-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The cross-species empirical relationship can be tested well with public egg and body-size data. The mechanistic explanation by oviduct pressure is only indirectly discriminated, but the central 'common rule' is resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across bird species, relate quantitative egg asymmetry and posterior taper to egg volume divided by adult female body size, controlling phylogeny and ecology. A robust positive association supports the empirical rule; no association refutes it, while direct oviduct dimensions would be needed for the pressure explanation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Oviduct size and in vivo pressure are generally absent.

Phylogeny, flight ecology and clutch strategy confound the association.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparative rule, that the most tapered eggs are large relative to the parent, can be fit directly to open shape and adult-size data spanning most bird orders. Those same datasets have already been used to compare anatomical and incubation correlates, so the pattern is resolvable and the pressure mechanism is only proxied. A positive size–asymmetry slope would support the rule Thompson states and would still leave rival causes of taper in play.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress egg asymmetry on egg size relative to adult body size across species, with a phylogenetic control, and inspect named cases such as guillemots, sandpipers, terns, and Apteryx. The common rule is supported by a positive relationship and by the stated exceptions having large oviducts; the pressure explanation is not tested unless oviduct pressure, rather than relative size alone, is measured.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Oviduct dimensions in the open file are not pressure records along the forming egg.

Relative size is a proxy for the pressure Thompson invokes, and flight or nesting correlates can produce the same pattern.
